Let $\pi:E\to M$ be a smooth rank-$r$ vector bundle and let
$\Phi_\alpha:\pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\to U_\alpha\times\mathbb R^r$ be a local
trivialization whose restriction on each fibre is a linear isomorphism. The
pair $(U_\alpha,\Phi_\alpha)$ is a **vector bundle chart**.

For two vector bundle charts $(U_\alpha,\Phi_\alpha)$ and
$(U_\beta,\Phi_\beta)$, the overlap map

$$\Phi_\beta\circ\Phi_\alpha^{-1}:(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta)\times\mathbb R^r\to (U_\alpha\cap U_\beta)\times\mathbb R^r$$

has the form

$$\Phi_\beta\circ\Phi_\alpha^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\beta\alpha}(p)v),$$

where $g_{\beta\alpha}:U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\to GL(r,\mathbb R)$ is smooth. The
map $g_{\beta\alpha}$ is the **transition function** from chart $\alpha$ to
chart $\beta$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $M$. A family of smooth functions $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$ with $\phi_i:M\to [0,1]$ is a **smooth partition of unity subordinate to** $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ when:

1. the family $(\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i))_{i\in I}$ is locally finite;
2. $\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i)\subseteq U_i$ for every $i\in I$; and
3. $\sum_i \phi_i(p)=1$ for every $p\in M$.

derivations.claim: If $X$ is empty, take the unique empty family. If $M$ is empty, its bundle has the unique empty smooth section, and take the unique family of those sections. In either case all agreement constraints and the straight-line homotopy hold vacuously, and the displayed error is $\sup\{0\}=0$. We may therefore assume $X$ and $M$ nonempty. Choose a finite bundle atlas and a subordinate finite smooth partition of unity using compactness and [F1, F2]. In each chart multiply a section coefficient by its partition function, extend by zero within the chart, convolve with a fixed compactly supported smooth mollifier of radius $\delta$, and sum the finitely many resulting local sections. For each $\delta>0$ this defines a linear operator $S_\delta:C^0(M,E)\to\Gamma^\infty(E)$: every output derivative is an integral of the input against a derivative of a fixed smooth kernel, so each $C^r$ seminorm is bounded by a finite constant times the input $C^0$ norm. Uniform continuity of each input on compact chart supports gives $\|S_\delta u-u\|_{C^0}\to0$ for every $u$. Since $x\mapsto s(x,\cdot)$ has compact image in $C^0(M,E)$, a finite subcover argument makes this convergence uniform over $x\in X$.

The family $x\mapsto S_\delta s(x,\cdot)$ is continuous into $C^\infty$ by the seminorm bounds in step 1.1. Let $U$ be the chosen collar neighborhood of $K$, with projection $r:U\to K$, and choose a continuous cutoff $\chi:X\to[0,1]$ equal to $1$ on $K$ and supported inside $U$. For an interior hypersurface use the two-sided collar $c:K\times(-2a,2a)\to U$, $r(c(k,t))=k$, with $\chi$ supported in $|t|<a$; no boundary of $X$ is needed. Set
$$s_1(x)=S_\delta s(x)+\chi(x)\bigl(s(r(x))-S_\delta s(r(x))\bigr)$$
on $U$ and $s_1=S_\delta s$ off $U$. Every term is a smooth section in $m$ and varies continuously in $C^\infty$ with $x$. At $x\in K$, $s_1(x)=s(x)$. As $x$ approaches $K$, continuity into $C^0$ and the uniform approximation in step 1.1 make the correction uniformly small; choose the collar width and then $\delta$ so $s_1$ remains arbitrarily $C^0$-close to $s$.

For each marked point choose a bundle chart and a smooth bump $b_i$ supported in that chart with $b_i(m_i)=1$; shrink the charts to be pairwise disjoint. In the chart extend $v_i-s_1(x,m_i)$ as the constant coefficient vector and multiply by $b_i$. The resulting correction $c_i(x,\cdot)$ is a smooth section continuous in $x$ in every $C^r$ seminorm, is zero on $K$ because $s_1=s=v_i$ there, and changes the value at $m_i$ by exactly $v_i-s_1(x,m_i)$. Put $\widetilde s=s_1+\sum_i c_i$. The finite corrections preserve $C^\infty$ continuity and the relative condition. Since the errors at the marked points are bounded by the uniform $C^0$ error from step 2.1 and the bumps have fixed bounded norms, choosing that error sufficiently small gives the prescribed $\varepsilon$ bound.

For $0\le t\le1$ define $H_t(x,m)=(1-t)s(x,m)+t\widetilde s(x,m)$ in the vector space $E_m$. This is continuous, equals $s$ at $t=0$ and $\widetilde s$ at $t=1$, and is constant on $K$ and at each marked point because both endpoint families agree there. Thus the required relative homotopy exists.

For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, the **unreduced mapping cylinder** is
$$M_f=(Y\amalg(X\times I))/((x,0)\sim f(x)).$$
Write $j:X\to M_f$, $j(x)=[x,1]$, and $r:M_f\to Y$, $r(y)=y$, $r([x,s])=f(x)$. The formula for r descends continuously by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The **unreduced mapping cone** is $C_f=M_f/j(X)$, collapsing the entire free end to a point when it is nonempty. If X is empty this quotient is Y, with no extra cone point adjoined. These constructions do not collapse a basepoint track. Reduced cones and suspensions are defined separately below. Deformations always use the homotopy convention in [[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]].

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

For a well-pointed CGWH based space $(X,x_0)$ set
$$CX=(X\times I)/(X\times\{1\}\cup\{x_0\}\times I),\qquad \Sigma X=CX/(X\times\{0\}).$$
The common collapsed set is the basepoint; the copy of X at height zero is the cone base. All products and mapping conventions are those of [[def-compactly-generated-conventions-for-based-homotopy]], and well-pointedness means [[def-cofibration-and-homotopy-extension-property]].

For a based $f:X\to Y$ put $C_f=Y\cup_f CX$, the **reduced homotopy cofiber**, with $i:Y\to C_f$ the inclusion and $q:C_f\to\Sigma X$ collapsing Y. This reduced notation is used in this item and its based consumers; it differs from the unreduced cone of [[def-mapping-cylinder-and-mapping-cone]]. A reduced cylinder also collapses the basepoint track. Maps on all these quotients are defined by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]].

Write $\rho_X([x,t])=[x,1-t]$ and $-\Sigma f=\rho_Y\Sigma f$. The cofiber sequence convention is
$$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{i}C_f\xrightarrow{q}\Sigma X\xrightarrow{-\Sigma f}\Sigma Y\xrightarrow{-\Sigma i}\Sigma C_f\xrightarrow{-\Sigma q}\Sigma^2X\xrightarrow{\Sigma^2 f}\Sigma^2Y\longrightarrow\cdots.$$
The homotopy equivalences and mapping-set exactness behind this notation are proved below; this definition does not assert a covariant exact sequence of homotopy groups.

For a space $X$ and commutative unital coefficient ring $R$, put
$$H^*(X;R)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^n(X;R),\qquad [\varphi]\smile[\psi]=[\varphi\smile\psi].$$
The groups and equality of representatives are those of [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]]. The multiplication descends through both quotient maps by [[thm-cup-product-leibniz-identity]], including simultaneous changes. Extend to finite sums of homogeneous classes by distributivity; only finitely many summands occur, so each product belongs to the displayed direct sum.

This is the **singular cohomology ring**. To check the ring assertion before using it, let $\varphi,\psi,\eta$ have degrees $p,q,r$. On an arbitrary $(p+q+r)$-simplex both parenthesizations of their cochain cup product evaluate to
$$\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p])\,\psi(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\,\eta(\sigma[p+q,\ldots,p+q+r]).$$
Restriction to a face and then a face of that face is restriction to the listed vertex block, and multiplication in $R$ is associative. Thus cochain associativity holds exactly and descends to classes. Bilinearity gives the two distributive laws. Addition, additive inverses and zero come from the abelian quotient groups. Products of degrees $p,q$ have degree $p+q$.

Its multiplicative unit is the class of the cochain $\mathbf1\in C^0(X;R)$ assigning $1_R$ to every singular vertex. On any edge, $\delta\mathbf1=1_R-1_R=0$. The front/back formula gives $\mathbf1\smile\varphi=\varphi=\varphi\smile\mathbf1$ on every simplex. This includes all components at once: degree-zero cochains need not have finite support on the set of vertices or components.

If $X$ is empty or $R=0$, the ring is the zero ring and its unit equals zero, as allowed by our unital-ring convention. The formula for three factors works also when any degree is zero and for degenerate simplices; for one-point $X$ it has the same unit. Nothing here chooses a representative for every class: the quotient operation is defined by representative independence. No AC is used.

Assume AC. For a CW pair $(X,A)$ and local system $\mathcal L$, the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients:
$$H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
For a connected pair, it is the equivariant-Hom complex on cellular chains after the published right chain action is converted to the left action $g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}$; equivalently its cochains satisfy $\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c)$. The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms.

Let $q : X \to Y$ be a quotient map ([[def-quotient-topology]]). Then:

1. **Characteristic property.** For every space $W$ and every function
   $k : Y \to W$,
   $$k \text{ is continuous } \iff k \circ q \text{ is continuous} .$$
2. **Factorisation.** Let $f : X \to W$ be continuous and **constant on the
   fibres of $q$**, that is $q(x) = q(x')$ implies $f(x) = f(x')$. Then there is
   exactly one function $\bar f : Y \to W$ with $\bar f \circ q = f$, and it is
   continuous.
3. **Composites.** If $q : X \to Y$ and $p : Y \to Z$ are quotient maps then
   $p \circ q : X \to Z$ is a quotient map.

The quotient projection

$$p:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,\qquad t\longmapsto[t],$$

is a universal covering space of the quotient circle, pointed by $0\mapsto[0]$.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

For every r≥1, degree is an isomorphism $\pi_r(S^r,b)\to\mathbb Z$, sending the identity to +1 and cubical concatenation, equivalently oriented pinch sum, to addition. Two based sphere self-maps are homotopic through based maps if and only if their degrees agree. No infinite choice principle is needed.

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

Let $f:S^3\to S^2$ be a based continuous map. Give $S^2$ an orientation and give the attached $4$-cell its chosen orientation. Its mapping cone is the CW complex $C_f=S^2\cup_fD^4$, with the basepoint as its $0$-cell. Let $x\in H^2(C_f;\mathbb Z)$ be the unique class restricting to the positive generator of $H^2(S^2;\mathbb Z)$, and let $y\in H^4(C_f;\mathbb Z)$ be the generator determined by the oriented $4$-cell. Define the integral mapping-cone Hopf invariant $H(f)\in\mathbb Z$ by the equation
$$x\smile x=H(f)y.$$

Assume AC. Every numerable fiber bundle, with its supplied ordinary local product charts and support-subordinate locally finite partition of unity, is a Hurewicz fibration in all ordinary spaces. In particular a bundle of CGWH spaces with these charts is a Hurewicz fibration in CGWH. AC is used to well-order the set of finite chart words. No selection of a chart for every base point or of a separate lift for every path is made.

For integers $0\le k<r$, $r\ge1$, every continuous based map $(S^k,a)\to(S^r,b)$ is nullhomotopic through maps fixing a. For k=0 this says every point of $S^r$ can be joined to b. No arbitrary choice principle is required.

Let

$$C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$$

with the Euclidean subspace topology. The function

$$h:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\longrightarrow C,\qquad h([t])=(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t),$$

is a homeomorphism. Thus $[t]\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to the unit circle and sends $[0]$ to $(1,0)$.

Let $G$ be an abelian group. For a based well-pointed space $X$—meaning that the basepoint inclusion
$\{x_0\}\hookrightarrow X$ is a cofibration—reduced singular homology has
natural isomorphisms
$\widetilde H_{n+1}(\Sigma X;G)\cong\widetilde H_n(X;G)$ for all integers $n$. Here $\Sigma X$ is the suspension with two distinct
apices, as in [[def-adjunction-cone-suspension]].

derivations.claim: The Hopf map is a locally trivial circle bundle: in the chart $z_0\ne0$ with $w=z_1/z_0$, the section is $(1,w)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}$ and the fiber coordinate is $z_0/|z_0|$; use $(w,1)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}$ and $z_1/|z_1|$ in the other chart. These formulas give continuous inverse bundle charts. Put $a_i([z])=|z_i|^2/(|z_0|^2+|z_1|^2)$, $b_i=\max(0,a_i-1/4)$ and $\rho_i=b_i/(b_0+b_1)$. At least one $a_i\ge1/2$, so the denominator is positive, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\subseteq\{a_i\ge1/4\}\subseteq\{z_i\ne0\}$. This is a finite numeration with closed supports subordinate to the charts. By [F6] the Hopf bundle is Hurewicz and hence Serre. By [F1], $\pi_2(S^1)=\pi_3(S^1)=0$; the LES [F2] therefore makes $h_*:\pi_3(S^3)\to\pi_3(S^2)$ an isomorphism. By [F3] its source is generated by the identity, so $[h]$ generates $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$.

Write $\mathbb{CP}^2=\{[z_0:z_1:z_2]\}$ and use the open cell $z_2\ne0$ with representative $(w_0,w_1,1)$, $w\in\mathbb C^2$. Its characteristic disk can be taken as the unit ball in $\mathbb C^2$ via $w\mapsto[w_0:w_1:\sqrt{1-|w|^2}]$; the interior parametrizes the complement of $\mathbb{CP}^1$, and on $|w|=1$ the boundary map is $[w_0:w_1]=h(w)$. Thus $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is the mapping cone $C_h$. By [F4], the degree-two generator squares to the degree-four generator, so [F5] gives $H(h)=1$.

Let $d_m:S^3\to S^3$ have degree $m$. The radial cone extension $D^4\to D^4$, $ru\mapsto r d_m(u)$, has relative degree $m$ and boundary $d_m$: on collapsing the disk boundary its map is $\Sigma d_m$, whose degree is $m$ by the natural homology suspension in [F6]. Together with the identity on $S^2$, it defines a map $C_{h\circ d_m}\to C_h$, since the boundary attaching maps agree. It pulls the degree-two generator of $C_h$ back to that of $C_{h\circ d_m}$ and the degree-four generator back to $m$ times the latter. Pulling back $x_h^2=y_h$ therefore gives $x_{h\circ d_m}^2=m y_{h\circ d_m}$, which is exactly $H(h\circ d_m)=m$ by [F5].

The coefficient $H(f)$ is invariant under a based homotopy $H_t$ of attaching maps. A comparison $C_{f_0}\to C_{f_1}$ is the identity on $S^2$; on a cone point $[x,t]$ it equals $H_{2t}(x)$ for $0\le t\le1/2$ and the target cone point $[x,2t-1]$ for $1/2\le t\le1$. The formulas agree at the seam, respect the tip, and are continuous by quotient descent. Reversing the homotopy gives its homotopy inverse: the composites insert a path followed by its reverse, which contracts by shrinking its traversed homotopy parameter, and then a linear cone reparametrization removes the constant collar. Both maps restrict to the identity on the bottom sphere and have relative top-cell degree $+1$, so cup-product naturality preserves $H$. Since step 1.1 identifies every homotopy class with $[h\circ d_m]$ for a unique integer $m$, step 2.1 implies that any attachment with $H(f)=m$ has class $m[h]$.

citations.quote: Let $h:S^3\to\mathbb{CP}^1\cong S^2$ be the Hopf map $h(z_0,z_1)=[z_0:z_1]$ on the unit sphere in $\mathbb C^2$. Then $h$ generates $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z$. Use the integral mapping-cone Hopf invariant $H(f)$ defined for based maps $f:S^3\to S^2$ by $x^2=H(f)y$ in $C_f=S^2\cup_fD^4$, with the positive degree-two and oriented top-cell generators. With the complex orientations, $C_h\cong\mathbb{CP}^2$, $H(h)=1$, and for every integer $m$ and degree-$m$ map $d_m:S^3\to S^3$, $H(h\circ d_m)=m$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. Give the graded tensor product the multiplication
$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=(-1)^{|b||a'|}(a\smile a')\otimes(b\smile b').$$
For arbitrary spaces $X,Y$, external product $a\times b=\operatorname{pr}_X^*a\smile\operatorname{pr}_Y^*b$ gives a unital graded-ring homomorphism to $H^*(X\times Y;R)$. This multiplicativity requires no AC.

Assume in addition AC, that $R$ is a PID, and that either every $H_q(Y;R)$ or every $H_p(X;R)$ is finite free over $R$. Then this homomorphism is an isomorphism.

For CW pairs $(X,A),(Y,B)$ with supplied characteristic maps, relative external product is likewise a graded-ring homomorphism
$$H^*(X,A;R)\mathbin{\widehat\otimes}_R H^*(Y,B;R)\longrightarrow H^*(X\times Y,(A\times Y)\cup(X\times B);R),$$
where the hat denotes the displayed graded multiplication on the ordinary graded direct-sum tensor product, not a completion. Relative rings need not have units. This relative multiplicativity is choice-free for every commutative unital $R$. Under AC and the PID hypothesis it is an isomorphism if either every $H_q(Y,B;R)$ or every $H_p(X,A;R)$ is finite free. Neither additive assertion requires bounded dimension or finite-rank singular chain groups. Products have their ordinary product topologies; AC enters only in additive bijectivity.

Let $(Z,z_0)$ be a based topological space. Define its reduced suspension as $\Sigma Z=(Z\times[0,1])/(Z\times\{0,1\}\cup\{z_0\}\times[0,1])$, with the collapsed subset as basepoint. Let $\iota_1,\iota_2:\Sigma Z\to\Sigma Z\vee\Sigma Z$ be the wedge inclusions. The reduced suspension pinch map $p_Z:\Sigma Z\to\Sigma Z\vee\Sigma Z$ is induced by
$$p_Z([z,t])=\begin{cases}\iota_1([z,2t]),&0\le t\le\tfrac12,\\\iota_2([z,2t-1]),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$
At $t=\tfrac12$ both values are the wedge basepoint.

derivations.claim: Let $a,b\in H^2(S^2\times S^2;\mathbb Z)$ be the positive generators from the two projections. By [F2], $a^2=b^2=0$ and $ab$ is the positive top generator. The map $\nabla:W\to S^2$ extends over the cone on $\beta$ by the definition $\beta=\nabla\alpha$; hence it extends to a map $q:S^2\times S^2=W\cup_\alpha D^4\to C_\beta$. On $W$, $q$ is the fold into the bottom $S^2$ of $C_\beta$, so $q^*x=a+b$. On the open $4$-cell, the extension is the characteristic disk of $C_\beta$ with degree $+1$ by [A1], so $q^*y=ab$.

Let $i:W\hookrightarrow S^2\times S^2$ be the $2$-skeleton inclusion. The characteristic disk extends $i\alpha$ over $D^4$, so $\Sigma i\circ\Sigma\alpha$ is null. Define
$$r=(\Sigma p_1\vee\Sigma p_2)\circ\operatorname{pinch}:\Sigma(S^2\times S^2)\longrightarrow\Sigma S^2\vee\Sigma S^2,$$
where $p_1,p_2$ are the projections and the pinch is [F3]. On the first suspended wedge summand, the first projection branch is the identity up to linear rescaling of the suspension coordinate and the second branch is constant; on the second summand the roles reverse. Thus $r\circ\Sigma i\simeq\operatorname{id}_{\Sigma W}$. Applying $r$ to the nullhomotopy in the first sentence gives $\Sigma\alpha\simeq *$. Composing with $\Sigma\nabla$ gives $\Sigma\beta\simeq *$.

In the cone $C_\beta$, $x^2=H(\beta)y$ by [F1]. Pulling back with step 1.1 yields $(a+b)^2=H(\beta)ab$. Since $a^2=b^2=0$ and degree-two classes commute, the left side is $2ab$. The class $ab$ is a generator, so $H(\beta)=2$.

For based maps $a,b:S^3\to S^2$, the group operation on $\pi_3(S^2)$ is represented by $(a\vee b)\circ p_{S^2}$, where $p_{S^2}:\Sigma S^2\to\Sigma S^2\vee\Sigma S^2$ is the pinch in [F3]; the operation on $\pi_4(S^3)$ is represented by $p_{S^3}:\Sigma S^3\to\Sigma S^3\vee\Sigma S^3$. In the quotient model $\Sigma^2 Z=(Z\times[0,1]^2)/\!\sim$, the map $\Sigma p_Z$ pinches one suspension coordinate and $p_{\Sigma Z}$ pinches the other. Write the square of suspension coordinates as a disk with its boundary collapsed. For each angle $\theta$, split the disk by the diameter at angle $\theta$, map the two half-disks to the two wedge summands using their boundary-collapsing rescalings to a full disk, and keep the first and second summands in that order. Choose these rescalings by rotating fixed rescalings of the two half-disks, so they vary continuously with $\theta$. As the diameter turns through a right angle, this gives a based homotopy between the two coordinate pinches; smashing this homotopy with $Z$ proves $\Sigma p_Z\simeq p_{\Sigma Z}$. Taking $Z=S^2$ and using $\Sigma S^2\cong S^3$ gives $\Sigma p_{S^2}\simeq p_{S^3}$. Since suspension preserves composition and sends a wedge of maps to the wedge of their suspensions, this compatibility gives $[\Sigma(a+b)]=[\Sigma a]+[\Sigma b]$; hence $E:[a]\mapsto[\Sigma a]$ is a homomorphism on $\pi_3(S^2)$. Now [F1, step 2.1] gives $[\beta]=2[h]$, so $[\Sigma\beta]=E([\beta])=2E([h])=2[\Sigma h]$. Since $\Sigma\beta$ is null by step 1.2, $2[\eta_3]=0$ for $\eta_3=\Sigma h$.

Assume AC. For every integer $n\geq0$,
$$H^*(\mathbb {CP}^n;\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[c_n]/(c_n^{n+1}),\qquad |c_n|=2,$$
where $c_n$ is reduction modulo two of the normalized integral generator. Also
$$H^*(\mathbb {CP}^{\infty};\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[c],\qquad |c|=2.$$
All odd cohomology groups vanish. Standard skeletal restrictions preserve the
named generators and are isomorphisms in every degree at most twice the
complex dimension of the finite target.

For every integer $k$, $Sq^k$ is independent of the cocycle representative and
of the chosen coherently carried higher-diagonal system. It is additive and
natural for maps of spaces and pairs. Thus

$$
Sq^k\colon H^n(X,A;\mathbb F_2)\longrightarrow H^{n+k}(X,A;\mathbb F_2)
$$

is a natural homomorphism, with the outside-range values fixed to zero by the
definition.

For $x\in H^n(X;\mathbb F_2)$,

$$
Sq^0x=x,\qquad Sq^k x=0\ \text{if }k>n,\qquad Sq^n x=x\smile x.
$$

The same assertions hold relatively. On reduced cohomology of based CW
complexes, every square commutes with the standard cohomology suspension:

$$
Sq^k(\sigma x)=\sigma(Sq^k x).
$$

Assume AC. Let $a,b$ be positive integers with $0<a<2b$. For every space
$X$, every $q\geq0$, and every $x\in H^q(X;\mathbb F_2)$,

$$Sq^aSq^b(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor a/2\rfloor}\binom{b-j-1}{a-2j}Sq^{a+b-j}Sq^j(x).$$

The binomial coefficients are reduced modulo two. A binomial coefficient is
zero when its lower index is negative or exceeds its nonnegative upper index,
and a Steenrod square with an index outside its defining nonnegative range is
zero.

Assume AC. For a CW pair $(X,A)$ and local system $\mathcal L$, the cellular cochain complex obtained from the skeletal filtration computes singular cohomology with local coefficients:
$$H^n\bigl(C^*_{\mathrm{cell}}(X,A;\mathcal L)\bigr)\cong H^n(X,A;\mathcal L).$$
For a connected pair, it is the equivariant-Hom complex on cellular chains after the published right chain action is converted to the left action $g\cdot c=c\cdot g^{-1}$; equivalently its cochains satisfy $\varphi(c\cdot g)=g^{-1}\varphi(c)$. The comparison is natural for cellular maps with correctly directed coefficient morphisms.

For a well-pointed CGWH based space $(X,x_0)$ set
$$CX=(X\times I)/(X\times\{1\}\cup\{x_0\}\times I),\qquad \Sigma X=CX/(X\times\{0\}).$$
The common collapsed set is the basepoint; the copy of X at height zero is the cone base. All products and mapping conventions are those of [[def-compactly-generated-conventions-for-based-homotopy]], and well-pointedness means [[def-cofibration-and-homotopy-extension-property]].

For a based $f:X\to Y$ put $C_f=Y\cup_f CX$, the **reduced homotopy cofiber**, with $i:Y\to C_f$ the inclusion and $q:C_f\to\Sigma X$ collapsing Y. This reduced notation is used in this item and its based consumers; it differs from the unreduced cone of [[def-mapping-cylinder-and-mapping-cone]]. A reduced cylinder also collapses the basepoint track. Maps on all these quotients are defined by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]].

Write $\rho_X([x,t])=[x,1-t]$ and $-\Sigma f=\rho_Y\Sigma f$. The cofiber sequence convention is
$$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{i}C_f\xrightarrow{q}\Sigma X\xrightarrow{-\Sigma f}\Sigma Y\xrightarrow{-\Sigma i}\Sigma C_f\xrightarrow{-\Sigma q}\Sigma^2X\xrightarrow{\Sigma^2 f}\Sigma^2Y\longrightarrow\cdots.$$
The homotopy equivalences and mapping-set exactness behind this notation are proved below; this definition does not assert a covariant exact sequence of homotopy groups.

For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, the **unreduced mapping cylinder** is
$$M_f=(Y\amalg(X\times I))/((x,0)\sim f(x)).$$
Write $j:X\to M_f$, $j(x)=[x,1]$, and $r:M_f\to Y$, $r(y)=y$, $r([x,s])=f(x)$. The formula for r descends continuously by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The **unreduced mapping cone** is $C_f=M_f/j(X)$, collapsing the entire free end to a point when it is nonempty. If X is empty this quotient is Y, with no extra cone point adjoined. These constructions do not collapse a basepoint track. Reduced cones and suspensions are defined separately below. Deformations always use the homotopy convention in [[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]].

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $C_{\eta_2}=\mathbb{CP}^2$ and $Sq^2$ sends its bottom degree-two generator to the nonzero degree-four class by [F2]. For reduced cones, suspension commutes with this cell cofiber: both $\Sigma C_f$ and $C_{\Sigma f}$ are the quotient of $I\times S^n\sqcup I\times S^{n+1}\times I$ by the same relations, collapsing suspension ends, cone tips and based tracks and identifying $(s,x,0)$ with $(s,f(x))$. Quotient descent therefore gives inverse continuous comparison maps. By [F5], ordinary cones are based homotopy equivalent to these reduced cones. Thus for every $n\ge2$ there is a based equivalence $C_{\eta_n}\simeq\Sigma^{n-2}C_h$, preserving the bottom and top cohomology classes. Suspension compatibility in [F2] therefore gives a nonzero $Sq^2:H^n(C_{\eta_n};\mathbb F_2)\to H^{n+2}(C_{\eta_n};\mathbb F_2)$.

Suppose for contradiction that $\eta_n\eta_{n+1}$ is null. Put $f=\eta_n:S^{n+1}\to S^n$ and $g=\eta_{n+1}:S^{n+2}\to S^{n+1}$. Let $K:CS^{n+2}\to S^n$ be a based cone extension of $f\circ g$, and let $\chi:CS^{n+1}\to C_f$ be the characteristic map of the cell attached by $f$. Decompose $S^{n+3}$ into two cones on $S^{n+2}$. On the first define $k:S^{n+3}\to C_f$ by $\chi\circ Cg$; on the second define it by $K$ followed by $S^n\hookrightarrow C_f$. On the common equator both formulas equal $f\circ g$, and on the chosen basepoint both equal the target basepoint, so they paste to a based continuous map. Attach an $(n+4)$-cell along $k$, obtaining $X=C_f\cup_kD^{n+4}$. Its cells have dimensions $0,n,n+2,n+4$. Collapsing the bottom $S^n$ gives an attaching map $\bar k=(\Sigma g)\circ c$, where $c:S^{n+3}\to S^{n+3}$ collapses the hemisphere carrying $K$ and expands the other hemisphere. In suspension coordinates $[x,s]$, $-1\le s\le1$, take $c[x,s]=[x,\varphi(s)]$, where $\varphi(s)=-1$ for $s\le0$ and $\varphi(s)=2s-1$ for $s\ge0$. The coordinate maps $\varphi_t(s)=(1-t)s+t\varphi(s)$ preserve the endpoints and give a based homotopy from the identity to $c$. Hence $\bar k$ is based homotopic to $\Sigma g=\eta_{n+2}$. An attaching homotopy $H$ induces a cone comparison equal to the identity on the bottom sphere, equal to $H(x,2t)$ on the first half of the cone, and equal to the target cone point $[x,2t-1]$ on the second half. The reverse homotopy gives an inverse up to homotopy by cancelling the traversed homotopy and its reverse. This comparison has degree $+1$ on the relative top cell. Consequently $X/S^n\simeq C_{\eta_{n+2}}$ by a based homotopy equivalence preserving both upper cellular generators. No covariant homotopy exact sequence for cofibers is assumed.

The cells of $X$ have dimensions $0,n,n+2,n+4$, so its cellular cochain differential is zero and $H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb F_2)=0$. Let $x,y,z$ denote the nonzero classes in degrees $n,n+2,n+4$, respectively. Inclusion $C_{\eta_n}\hookrightarrow X$ induces isomorphisms in degrees $n$ and $n+2$, since these cellular cochain groups and their differentials are unchanged by the single top cell. By step 1.1 and naturality [F2], $Sq^2x=y$. The based equivalence $X/S^n\simeq C_{\eta_{n+2}}$ from step 1.2 preserves the upper generators, so the quotient has nonzero $Sq^2$ between degrees $n+2$ and $n+4$ by step 1.1 at index $n+2$. Collapsing the bottom subcomplex removes precisely its $0$- and $n$-cells from the cellular cochains; the quotient map preserves the upper cellular generators and their differentials. Naturality [F2] therefore gives $Sq^2y=z$. Thus $Sq^2Sq^2x=z\ne0$. But $H^{n+1}(X;\mathbb F_2)=0$, so $Sq^1x=0$.
On the other hand, [F3] gives $Sq^2Sq^2x=Sq^3Sq^1x=0$ by step 2.1. This contradicts $Sq^2Sq^2x=z\ne0$, so the assumed null composite is impossible. Hence $\eta_n\eta_{n+1}\ne0$ for every $n\ge2$.

A **locally trivial fiber bundle with fiber $F$** is a continuous map $p:E\to B$, an open cover $(U_i)_{i\in S}$ of $B$, and homeomorphisms
$$\theta_i:p^{-1}(U_i)\longrightarrow U_i\times F,\qquad \operatorname{pr}_1\theta_i=p|_{p^{-1}(U_i)}.$$
Here bundle charts, including those used later for principal and associated bundles, are charts in ordinary topological spaces with ordinary product and subspace topologies. A bundle whose spaces are CGWH in addition can be considered in the CGWH fibration convention; we do not silently replace an ordinary product chart by a weaker k-product-chart assumption. Products and homeomorphisms have the meanings of [[thm-product-universal-property]] and [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]].

On $U_i\cap U_j$, the coordinate change has the form $(b,x)\mapsto(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$, with continuous inverse $(b,y)\mapsto(b,g_{ij}(b,y))$. In particular each $g_{ji}(b,-)$ is a homeomorphism of $F$. The identities $g_{ii}(b,x)=x$ and $g_{ki}(b,x)=g_{kj}(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$ hold because the corresponding chart composites cancel. No topology on a homeomorphism group of $F$ is assumed.

The bundle is **numerable** when the data include a partition $(\rho_i:B\to[0,1])_{i\in S}$ with locally finite cozero sets, sum one, and
$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho_i)=\overline{\{b:\rho_i(b)>0\}}\subseteq U_i.$$
This is the support-subordinate convention of [[def-partition-of-unity-subordinate-to-a-cover]]. Repeating a chart with multiple indices is allowed, so a partition subordinate to a refinement can be accompanied by an explicitly assigned original chart. Merely having pointwise finite sums or cozero containment is not this specified numerating data.

An empty base forces $E$ empty and allows the empty cover and partition. The fiber $F$ may be empty: then every chart domain, hence $E$, is empty even when $B$ is nonempty. When $F$ is nonempty the charts imply surjectivity by taking one point in the chart fiber for each particular base point; this assertion does not require choosing a simultaneous section. Over a point a chart identifies $E$ with $F$. No AC is assumed in the definition.

Assume AC. Every numerable fiber bundle, with its supplied ordinary local product charts and support-subordinate locally finite partition of unity, is a Hurewicz fibration in all ordinary spaces. In particular a bundle of CGWH spaces with these charts is a Hurewicz fibration in CGWH. AC is used to well-order the set of finite chart words. No selection of a chart for every base point or of a separate lift for every path is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $M$. A family of smooth functions $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$ with $\phi_i:M\to [0,1]$ is a **smooth partition of unity subordinate to** $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ when:

1. the family $(\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i))_{i\in I}$ is locally finite;
2. $\operatorname{supp}(\phi_i)\subseteq U_i$ for every $i\in I$; and
3. $\sum_i \phi_i(p)=1$ for every $p\in M$.

derivations.claim: Fix $v_0\in S^{2N-1}$. Choose an orthonormal basis $w_1,\ldots,w_{N-1}$ of $v_0^\perp$ so the matrix $(w_1,\ldots,w_{N-1},v_0)$ has determinant $1$. For $v$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood $U$ of $v_0$, project each $w_i$ onto $v^\perp$ and apply Gram–Schmidt in that fixed order. The projected vectors remain linearly independent after shrinking $U$, because their Gram determinant is continuous and equals $1$ at $v_0$. The resulting orthonormal frame depends smoothly on $v$. Multiply its first vector by the inverse of the determinant of the frame if necessary; this scalar has modulus one and the adjustment is smooth, preserves orthonormality, and makes the determinant exactly one. Thus $s(v)\in SU(N)$ is a smooth local section of $p$ on $U$.

For $g\in p^{-1}(U)$ with last column $v$, the matrix $s(v)^{-1}g$ fixes the last basis vector. Unitarity makes its orthogonal complement invariant, so it is block diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(A,1)$; determinant one gives $A\in SU(N-1)$. The maps
$$(A,v)\longmapsto s(v)\operatorname{diag}(A,1),\qquad g\longmapsto(\operatorname{upperBlock}(s(p(g))^{-1}g),p(g))$$
are smooth inverses between $SU(N-1)\times U$ and $p^{-1}(U)$. This proves local triviality with the asserted fiber.

The sphere is compact, so finitely many such neighborhoods cover it; [F2] gives a smooth partition of unity and hence a numeration. Applying [F1] proves the bundle is a Hurewicz fibration. For each parameter and each $t\in[0,1]$, the straight segment from the original matrix section to its close approximation stays in the tubular neighborhood: every point on the segment is within the approximation error of the original $SU(N)$ value. A **locally trivial fiber bundle with fiber $F$** is a continuous map $p:E\to B$, an open cover $(U_i)_{i\in S}$ of $B$, and homeomorphisms
$$\theta_i:p^{-1}(U_i)\longrightarrow U_i\times F,\qquad \operatorname{pr}_1\theta_i=p|_{p^{-1}(U_i)}.$$
Here bundle charts, including those used later for principal and associated bundles, are charts in ordinary topological spaces with ordinary product and subspace topologies. A bundle whose spaces are CGWH in addition can be considered in the CGWH fibration convention; we do not silently replace an ordinary product chart by a weaker k-product-chart assumption. Products and homeomorphisms have the meanings of [[thm-product-universal-property]] and [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]].

On $U_i\cap U_j$, the coordinate change has the form $(b,x)\mapsto(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$, with continuous inverse $(b,y)\mapsto(b,g_{ij}(b,y))$. In particular each $g_{ji}(b,-)$ is a homeomorphism of $F$. The identities $g_{ii}(b,x)=x$ and $g_{ki}(b,x)=g_{kj}(b,g_{ji}(b,x))$ hold because the corresponding chart composites cancel. No topology on a homeomorphism group of $F$ is assumed.

The bundle is **numerable** when the data include a partition $(\rho_i:B\to[0,1])_{i\in S}$ with locally finite cozero sets, sum one, and
$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho_i)=\overline{\{b:\rho_i(b)>0\}}\subseteq U_i.$$
This is the support-subordinate convention of [[def-partition-of-unity-subordinate-to-a-cover]]. Repeating a chart with multiple indices is allowed, so a partition subordinate to a refinement can be accompanied by an explicitly assigned original chart. Merely having pointwise finite sums or cozero containment is not this specified numerating data.

An empty base forces $E$ empty and allows the empty cover and partition. The fiber $F$ may be empty: then every chart domain, hence $E$, is empty even when $B$ is nonempty. When $F$ is nonempty the charts imply surjectivity by taking one point in the chart fiber for each particular base point; this assertion does not require choosing a simultaneous section. Over a point a chart identifies $E$ with $F$. No AC is assumed in the definition.

In particular a bundle of CGWH spaces with these charts is a Hurewicz fibration in CGWH. AC is used to well-order the set of finite chart words. derivations.claim: Define $\Phi:B\times H\to E$ by $\Phi(b,h)=s(b)h$. Every $e\in E$ lies over a unique $b=p(e)$ and the principal action is free and transitive on $p^{-1}(b)$, so there is a unique $h$ with $e=s(b)h$. Thus $\Phi$ is bijective. In each local principal chart, $s$ is a continuous local section and the group coordinate $h$ is continuous; these charts cover $B$, so the inverse $e\mapsto(p(e),h(e))$ is continuous. The forward map is continuous by the action. Hence $\Phi$ is a homeomorphism.

Fix $b_0\in B$. Under $\Phi$, the inclusion $i:H\to E$, $h\mapsto s(b_0)h$, and the map $r:E\to H$, $r(e)=\operatorname{pr}_H(\Phi^{-1}(e))$, satisfy $r\circ i=\operatorname{id}_H$. Thus $H$ is a retract. If $E$ is weakly contractible, it is path connected by [A1], so its continuous image $r(E)=H$ is path connected.

Choose basepoint $e_0=s(b_0)$. The maps $i$ and $r$ are based and [F2] gives $r_*i_*=(r\circ i)_*=\operatorname{id}_{\pi_j(H,e)}$. But $\pi_j(E,e_0)=0$ by [A1], so $i_*$ has zero target; the identity on $\pi_j(H,e)$ factors through zero and is zero. Therefore $\pi_j(H,e)=0$ for each $j\ge1$.

Let $P\to S^r$ be any smooth principal $SU(N)$ bundle, where $r=3$ or $4$ and $N\ge2$. Fix a point $m\in S^r$ and a frame $p_m\in P_m$. Write $\mathcal G_{\infty,m}(P)=\{u\in\mathcal G_\infty(P):u(p_m)=e\}$ for the based subgroup of the smooth gauge group defined by finite-atlas $C^\infty$ derivative seminorms; for brevity put $\mathcal G_m(P):=\mathcal G_{\infty,m}(P)$. For every $j\ge1$ there is a group isomorphism
$$\pi_j(\mathcal G_m(P),e)\cong\pi_{j+r}(SU(N),e),$$
and there is a bijection of pointed component sets $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P),e)\cong\pi_r(SU(N),e)$. These identifications are independent of the clutching class of $P$; the unbased evaluation fibration may still depend on that class.

For every $N\ge2$, $SU(N)$ is path connected, $\pi_1(SU(N))=\pi_2(SU(N))=0$, and $\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. In addition, $\pi_4(SU(2))\cong\mathbb Z/2$ is finite and $\pi_5(SU(2))\ne0$. Here $SU(2)\cong S^3$ by the map sending a unit quaternion to its defining special-unitary matrix.

For every r≥1, degree is an isomorphism $\pi_r(S^r,b)\to\mathbb Z$, sending the identity to +1 and cubical concatenation, equivalently oriented pinch sum, to addition. Two based sphere self-maps are homotopic through based maps if and only if their degrees agree. No infinite choice principle is needed.

Let $r\in\{3,4\}$, $N\ge2$, and $P\to S^r$ be any smooth principal $SU(N)$ bundle. Write $\mathcal G(P):=\mathcal G_\infty(P)$ for its smooth gauge group with the finite-atlas $C^\infty$ section topology and $\overline{\mathcal G}(P):=\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty(P)=\mathcal G_\infty(P)/Z_N$ for the quotient by constant central gauge sections. Then either $\overline{\mathcal G}(P)$ has more than one path component or at least one of its based homotopy groups $\pi_j(\overline{\mathcal G}(P),e)$, $j\ge1$, is nonzero. More precisely, for $r=3$ it has infinitely many path components, and for $r=4$ its fundamental group is nontrivial.

Let $\mathcal A_\infty:=A_0+\Omega^1(M,\operatorname{ad}P)$ and let $\mathcal G_\infty:=\Gamma^\infty(\operatorname{Ad}P)$ be the group of smooth adjoint-group sections under pointwise multiplication, identified above with the smooth gauge group. Give it the $C^\infty$ section topology generated by all finite-atlas derivative seminorms. Define $\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty:=\mathcal G_\infty/Z_N$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected oriented boundaryless smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$, let $N\ge2$, let $P\to M$ be a smooth principal $SU(N)$ bundle, and fix a frame $p_m$ over $m\in M$. Use the adjoint group bundle $Ad(P)=P\times_{Ad}SU(N)$. Write $\mathcal G_\infty(P)$ for the smooth gauge group with its $C^\infty$ section topology as defined from finite-atlas derivative seminorms, and set $\mathcal G_{\infty,m}(P)=\{u\in\mathcal G_\infty(P):u(p_m)=e\}$. Define $\mathcal G^0(P)$ as the group of continuous sections of $Ad(P)$ with the compact-open topology and $\mathcal G^0_m(P)=\{u\in\mathcal G^0(P):u(p_m)=e\}$. Then the inclusions $\mathcal G_\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal G^0(P)$ and $\mathcal G_{\infty,m}(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal G^0_m(P)$ induce bijections on path components and isomorphisms on all homotopy groups at every basepoint. More precisely, finite sphere/disk parameter families and their relative homotopies have the same classes in the smooth and continuous section topologies.

derivations.claim: By [F2], each integer $k$ is represented by a based map $u_k:S^3\to SU(2)$ of degree $k$. The standard degree representative may be chosen smooth by a relative smooth approximation; [F5] then identifies its class with one in the smooth based section topology. Distinct integers give distinct elements of $\pi_3(SU(2))$ by degree classification, so [F1] proves that the based gauge group has components indexed by $\mathbb Z$.

The evaluation fibration has connected base $SU(2)$ and $\pi_1(SU(2))=0$ by [F2, F3]. Its component LES therefore identifies $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m)$ with $\pi_0(\mathcal G)$, so the full group also has infinitely many components. The quotient by $Z_2$ is a two-sheeted covering; [F6] shows its components are the orbits of the two-element deck action on the components upstairs. Each orbit has at most two members, so an infinite component set remains infinite after quotient; this instance is also the $r=3,N=2$ case of [F3].
